title: Our AI, Your Problem
gist: Bertrand Badré, Bruno Bouygues, and Ludovic Subran argue the real risk for Europe isn't choosing between a Chinese state-directed AI model and a US private-firm model, but that Europe has no seat at either table, echoing the 1971 'our currency, but your problem' dollar shock, and must build a third AI option to preserve its sovereignty.

themes.theme: Europe's absent seat in the US-China AI race

insights.claim: The debate over whether European firms should use a Chinese state-directed AI model or one built by a private US firm threatens to distract from Europe's most pressing problem, which is that it has no seat at either table.
insights.speaker: BERTRAND BADRÉ
insights.so_what: Reframes the AI sovereignty debate for European policymakers and investors: the binary US-vs-China AI choice obscures the deeper strategic problem of European dependency on foreign AI infrastructure.
insights.quote: The debate over whether European firms should use a Chinese state-directed model or one built by a private US firm threatens to distract from Europe’s most pressing problem, which is that it has no seat at either table.

insights.claim: To preserve its own sovereignty, Europe must create a third AI option for itself rather than choosing between the US and Chinese models.
insights.speaker: BERTRAND BADRÉ
insights.so_what: Signals a policy push toward European sovereign AI investment; watch for EU industrial policy, funding initiatives, or champions positioned as a 'third way' in AI.
insights.quote: To preserve its own sovereignty, the continent must create a third option for itself.

insights.claim: In 1971, US Treasury Secretary John Connally told European finance ministers that the dollar was 'our currency, but your problem' after the Nixon administration suspended the dollar's convertibility into gold, forcing the rest of the world to absorb the shock.
insights.speaker: BERTRAND BADRÉ
insights.so_what: Used as the historical template for the authors' argument that AI infrastructure controlled by the US or China could similarly impose unilateral shocks on Europe.

insights.claim: The dollar precedent shows what happens when the global economy runs on a currency (or, by the authors' analogy, a technology) that most countries do not control and cannot influence.
insights.speaker: BERTRAND BADRÉ
insights.so_what: Draws a direct analogy between dollar dependency and prospective AI-infrastructure dependency, implying similar geopolitical leverage risk for countries reliant on foreign AI stacks.
